summary: Market wrap saying the Australian sharemarket shrugged off a positive Wall Street lead after hotter-than-expected inflation data raised the odds of another Reserve Bank rate rise. REITs and consumer staples fell, with Dexus, Woolworths and Magellan in the news, while iron ore miners were supported. On Wall Street, big tech earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet were the focus, with oil falling on easing Israel-Hamas escalation fears.
one_line: ASX fell on hot inflation data and rate rise fears, while Wall Street rose ahead of Microsoft and Alphabet earnings and oil slid.
key_facts: REITs fell 2 per cent on the ASX, with Mirvac down 3.7 per cent and Dexus down 3.3 per cent.
Dexus chief executive Darren Steinberg announced he would step down next year after 11 years at the helm; the remuneration report received a first strike at the annual meeting in Sydney.
Woolworths lost 2 per cent despite sales rising 5.3 per cent in the 14 weeks to October, and vowed to pass on easing costs for protein and fresh produce.
Magellan shares dropped 3.5 per cent after the abrupt departure of chief executive David George; chairman Andrew Formica said the board decided to 'just deal with it'.
GSFM strategist Stephen Miller said inflation data plus the RBA's October minutes made a November rate rise a 'near certainty'.
Iron ore prices rose 2.9 per cent overnight, supporting miners, as Xi Jinping stepped up support for China's economy with extra sovereign debt and a higher budget deficit ratio.
The S&P 500 closed 0.7 per cent higher, the Dow Jones added 0.6 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.9 per cent.
Microsoft shares rose 5 per cent after hours after sales jumped 13 per cent to $US56.5 billion and profits climbed 27 per cent to $US22.3 billion.
Alphabet shares fell 6 per cent after hours: revenue rose 11 per cent to $US76.7 billion and net income was $US19.7 billion, but Google cloud missed expectations.
Meta dropped after being sued by California and a dozen other US states over harmful youth marketing claims.
Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Nvidia make up about a quarter of the S&P 500's market cap, with earnings projected to jump 34 per cent.
The 10-year Treasury yield was little changed at 4.85 per cent; West Texas Intermediate fell 2.2 per cent to $US83.59 a barrel.
